title: Write a recursive function for Fibonacci number (base: `fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1`, recursive: `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)`).
shortTitle: Write a Recursive Function for Fibonacci Number

s1_definition.profdef: The Fibonacci sequence is a series where each number is the sum of the two preceding numbers, starting from zero and one. It has two base cases, fib of zero is zero and fib of one is one, and a recursive case where fib of N equals fib of N minus one plus fib of N minus two. The naive recursive version has exponential time complexity because it recomputes the same subproblems repeatedly, so in production we use memoization or an iterative approach.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India projecting the growth of a special recurring-deposit scheme where this month's bonus equals the sum of the previous two months' bonuses. Month zero has a bonus of zero, month one has a bonus of one unit, and every month after that the bonus is the sum of the previous two months. To know month N's bonus you need month N minus one and month N minus two, and to know those you keep going back until you reach the two known starting months.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the previous two, starting from zero and one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Fibonacci sequence is a series where each number is the sum of the two preceding numbers, starting from zero and one. It has two base cases, fib of zero is zero and fib of one is one, and a recursive case where fib of N equals fib of N minus one plus fib of N minus two. The naive recursive version has exponential time complexity because it recomputes the same subproblems repeatedly, so in production we use memoization or an iterative approach.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India projecting the growth of a special recurring-deposit scheme where this month's bonus equals the sum of the previous two months' bonuses. Month zero has a bonus of zero, month one has a bonus of one unit, and every month after that the bonus is the sum of the previous two months. To know month N's bonus you need month N minus one and month N minus two, and to know those you keep going back until you reach the two known starting months.

**One line to remember:** Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the previous two, starting from zero and one.

sections.s2_technical:
Fibonacci has two base cases instead of one because the recursive case needs two previous values to add. The base cases are `if (n == 0) return 0;` and `if (n == 1) return 1;`. The recursive case is `return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);` which makes two recursive calls and adds their results.

The critical thing to understand is efficiency. The naive recursion is terribly slow because it recomputes the same values over and over. Computing fib of five calls fib of four and fib of three, but fib of four also calls fib of three, so fib of three is computed twice, and lower values many more times. This leads to roughly 2 to the power N calls, which is exponential and unusable beyond about forty.

The professional fix is memoization. We keep a cache, compute each value once, and reuse it. For example `if (memo.containsKey(n)) return memo.get(n);` returns the stored answer instantly, and after computing we do `memo.put(n, result);`. This turns the exponential algorithm into a linear one. An even simpler production approach is a bottom-up loop that keeps only the last two values, using constant memory.

A senior-level point is that because Fibonacci numbers grow exponentially, they overflow a long around the ninety-third term, so for large N we use BigInteger. The naive recursive form is excellent for teaching the idea of overlapping subproblems and for motivating dynamic programming, which is why interviewers ask it, but it should never ship as-is for large inputs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India launches a loyalty bonus scheme where each month's reward points equal the sum of the previous two months' points, seeded with zero and one. A customer like Rajesh wants to see the projected points at month N. This is literally the Fibonacci recurrence — month N equals month N minus one plus month N minus two.

Problem 2 — If we compute this with naive recursion, the same months get recalculated thousands of times and the projection for a distant month becomes unbearably slow, which is unacceptable for a live banking screen. This is why we add memoization, computing each month once and caching it, turning a slow exponential calculation into a fast linear one.

In our mini-project we build a `FibonacciCalculator` that offers both a naive recursive method (to demonstrate the concept) and a memoized recursive method (the production version using BigInteger). The demo computes a few loyalty-point projections and shows the memoized version handling a large month instantly.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: compute the loyalty points for month 5 using naive recursion, then month 100 using memoization.

Step 1: We call `fibNaive(5)`. It is not a base case, so it calls `fibNaive(4)` and `fibNaive(3)` and adds them.

Step 2: `fibNaive(4)` calls `fibNaive(3)` and `fibNaive(2)`. Notice `fibNaive(3)` is now going to be computed more than once across the whole tree — this is the wasteful overlap.

Step 3: The calls keep branching until they reach `fibNaive(1)` returning one and `fibNaive(0)` returning zero, which are the base cases that stop each branch.

Step 4: The results add back up the tree: fib of two is one, fib of three is two, fib of four is three, and fib of five is five.

Step 5: For month 100 we call `fibMemo(100)`. The first time a month is needed it is computed and stored in the cache. The second time the same month is needed, it is returned instantly from the cache.

Step 6: Because each month is computed exactly once, the memoized version finishes in linear time and BigInteger holds the huge value exactly without overflow.

```
[2026-10-26 19:40:03] INFO    Month 0 loyalty points (naive): 0
[2026-10-26 19:40:03] INFO    Month 1 loyalty points (naive): 1
[2026-10-26 19:40:03] INFO    Month 5 loyalty points (naive): 5
[2026-10-26 19:40:03] INFO    Month 10 loyalty points (naive): 55
[2026-10-26 19:40:03] INFO    Month 100 loyalty points (memoized): 354224848179261915075
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Naive fib(5) — overlapping subproblems (slow)
                    fib(5)
                   /      \
              fib(4)      fib(3)
             /    \        /   \
        fib(3)  fib(2)  fib(2) fib(1)   ← fib(3), fib(2) recomputed
         ...     ...

  Memoized fib(100) — each value computed ONCE
    fib(2)=1 → cache
    fib(3)=2 → cache
    ...
    fib(100)=354224848179261915075   (linear time, BigInteger)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Fibonacci sequence is a series where every number is the sum of the two before it, starting from zero and one. It has two base cases, fib of zero is zero and fib of one is one, because the recursive case needs two previous values to add together, and the recursive case is fib of N equals fib of N minus one plus fib of N minus two.

The point I always make clear in an interview is efficiency, because this is the real reason the question is asked. The naive recursive version is beautifully simple but it is exponential, because it recomputes the same subproblems again and again. Computing a distant term this way would take an enormous amount of time. So in production I apply memoization: I keep a cache, compute each value exactly once, store it, and reuse it. That single change turns the exponential algorithm into a linear one.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this for a loyalty bonus scheme where each month's points equal the sum of the previous two months' points. A customer can ask for the projection at any month, and with naive recursion a far-off month would freeze the screen. With memoization each month is computed once and cached in Redis, so the projection returns instantly even for large months.

The senior-level nuances I add are two. First, Fibonacci numbers grow exponentially and overflow a long around the ninety-third term, so I use BigInteger to keep the value exact. Second, an even leaner approach is a bottom-up loop that keeps only the last two values and uses constant memory. I present the recursive version to show I understand overlapping subproblems and dynamic programming, but I make sure the interviewer knows which version I would actually ship.
